Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
schema.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
schema.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. **IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. # 101 Football Athletes, One Season: Volume and Impacts Tracked Non-Contact Injury

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") and co-authors analyzed one full season, preseason through regular season, in 101 American football athletes (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14]). The aim was not to predict injuries before a session but to identify the relationship between training-load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, so practitioners get an idea of associated risk (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]).

- **Metrics from inertial sensor units** (vendor not named in the transcript): total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts with three thresholds, and inertial movement analysis (IMA) with three thresholds (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:12] to [09:12]).
- **Injuries:** 29 non-contact time-loss injuries, mostly lower extremity, plus an oblique in a linebacker, a low back strain and an elbow strain in a defensive lineman who was learning a new position (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18] to [13:49]).
- **Models:** the best model within each metric group, then a joint model. The player load model used total player load and player load "very high"; the IMA and impacts models used all three bands; the joint model used total player load, player load low and impacts high and was "the most useful" for explaining injury (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49] to [14:20]).
- **Direction of effects:** total player load and impacts high carried the highest increase in risk; player load low had a decreased association (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20] to [15:22]). Ward reads total player load as volume and impacts high as session intensity or physicality, interesting because collision injuries were not studied (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51]).
- **Position group:** adding it as a categorical variable did not help in any model, and he suspects too few injuries per group (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22] to [15:53]).
- **Timing:** in Q&A, most injuries occurred in training camp, very few once the season started (TbYgc6_qQzo [22:05]).
- **Not shown:** effect sizes, thresholds or band values (the transcript gives none), and no game load (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:53]).

**Why it works** — Ward's interpretation for the inverse player-load-low result is that a session cannot be high and low intensity at the same time, so the inverse relation is "logical" (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why impacts would raise non-contact risk. Inference: it may reflect session physicality or camp-style practice, but the talk does not say.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a template for which Catapult columns to read beside the standard load view after practice (total volume, a high-intensity impacts count, and the low band) instead of one load number. Eric's baseline: core GPS metrics tracked include player load, field time and IMA for indoor sessions (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Eric's baseline: no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally ("They do not exist formally," Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7). Inference: this study supplies no thresholds to fill that gap. Inference: camp weeks, where most injuries fell here, are where a Baylor descriptive look would start.

**When NOT to apply** — One team, one season, 29 injuries, and no effect sizes. The talk does not name the team or level; a questioner refers to roster reduction to "a final 53" (TbYgc6_qQzo [21:35]), which suggests an NFL-style roster, but that is not confirmed. Association only, with no game load. Injury types were pooled across hamstring, adductor and other injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23] to [16:53]). Do not set a Baylor load limit from it, and do not change practice plans because one session scored high on impacts. Ward himself says thresholds "bounce around" between studies (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the defensive lineman's elbow extensor strain came while learning a new position and doing exercises unique to him in training (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the data were coded). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. [[claim--ima-informs-linemen-where-gps-distance-does-not]].

[04:36] there's a lack of censoring so frequently if let's say an athlete goes out completes maybe of the first quarter of a session and sustains an injury and has to be removed from that session oftentimes these these papers or the models that that are generated from these papers don't censor the athletes in those sessions so what happens as the model kicks out some weird outcome like really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries so the way that this data gets coded on the backend and handled on the back end is really really important these papers often will

# Case Study: Joe Thomas, Pass Block Win Rate and the Quarterback Who Held the Ball

**What it is** — Panelists describe how ESPN's pass block and pass rush win rates came about accidentally: a script written to find the closest defender on each pass, to answer researchers' repeated questions about separation, drew a visualization that showed who was blocking whom (teg9SfzpMy0 [14:59], [15:30]). # Spring training field lab: pitchers back from UCL surgery looked mechanically like never-injured pitchers

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig describes a study done with Major League Baseball in the 2014 spring training in Arizona and Florida, where his group brought the motion-capture lab (in a tent or outdoors) to the teams instead of bringing pitchers to Birmingham (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:16], [26:17]). Design: 40 pitchers who had had the surgery a couple of years earlier and had made it back to spring training, against 40 never-injured pitchers; each filled out a form, had range of motion measured lying on a table, then had a full kinematics and kinetics test (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:47], [26:17], [26:47]).

He named four hypotheses before looking (AgouMNTeyo4 [26:47], [27:18], [27:49], [28:21]):
- The returners show compensation, "messed up" elbow and shoulder mechanics.
- They hold back: stand more upright and push the elbow rather than driving as they did.
- The "inverted W": the arm is late and still down at foot contact, measured as arm external rotation at foot contact.
- A low elbow that is then raised, a stressful pattern.

Result: both groups threw about 85 mph in spring training and matched on height and weight; he found no difference in flexibility and no difference in mechanics (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21], [28:52]). His reading: minor leaguers who make it back have typical flexibility and mechanics, "when it works it works" (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22]).

**Why it works** — The design works because it names each hypothesis as a measurable pattern before testing; the speaker gives no mechanism for the null result. Inference: if returners were compensating, the group means would differ on the four named patterns, and they did not.

**When to apply** — As a template for a field comparison of a return group against matched controls: define the comparison group, name hypotheses as measurable patterns in advance, and take the lab to the athletes when the athletes cannot come to the lab.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's contribution to return to performance is "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4); assessment is repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April," Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). The baseline does not document a return-group comparison at Baylor.

**When NOT to apply** — Fleisig lists the limits himself: only minor leaguers were studied, only after they made it back (no pre-injury mechanics), and only success stories, not the "10 or 20%" who did not return (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]). A null result in 40 against 40 does not exclude small differences, and the talk gives no effect sizes. At the time of the talk the study had "just got published". # Bite Distance Under Expected Is Steadier Year to Year Than the Coverage Grade

**What it is** — Eric Eager (PFF) says PFF's linebacker coverage grade has been unstable, so great coverage players "don't always repeat that year to year" (Q3i3FOC-dPE [10:20], [10:51]). He builds a tracking trait instead: how far a linebacker's vertical (y) displacement moves on play action, adjusted for situation (how often the team runs inside or outside zone, down and distance; on third and 15 players don't bite, on first and 10 they do), then averaged over time (Q3i3FOC-dPE [11:22], [11:53]). He calls it bite distance under expected (BDU). His result: using R-squared, it is "about four times three or four times more predictive" year to year than the coverage grade; the caption multiple is garbled (Q3i3FOC-dPE [11:53], [12:23]). His stated reasoning: a linebacker who bites leaves the middle of the field, the most valuable area to throw, open (Q3i3FOC-dPE [10:51], [11:22]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that a fake handoff pulls the linebackers out of the middle zone (his example: two linebackers around the 27-yard line vacating after a fake handoff, Q3i3FOC-dPE [10:51]). He does not show that biting causes the coverage failures. Inference: the trait is steady because it measures a habit, not the outcome of a throw.

**When to apply** — When a graded outcome is unstable year to year and a repeatable behavior can be pulled from tracking data. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses percent change from baseline or a rolling average, with "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (Explicit). Inference: both prefer the steadier signal.

**When NOT to apply** — The multiple ("three or four times") is garbled in the captions and the R-squared values are not given (Q3i3FOC-dPE [12:23]). Fred Warner and other player names are used as "smell test" examples, and no group-level validation is shown beyond that (Q3i3FOC-dPE [11:53]). Caption spelling issues (for instance "luke lee" for the player the speaker calls a Hall of Famer) mean names should be checked. `untested`. A steady trait is not the same as a good one; see [[heuristic--read-linebacker-play-action-metrics-as-a-pair-with-run-cost]].

**Example** — The speaker's: Fred Warner's contract and a Hall of Fame-level player rate well on the metric; Neville Hewitt, whom the speaker calls "not a great linebacker," tops the list (Q3i3FOC-dPE [11:53], [19:28]).

# DeepQB Picks the Targeted Receiver About 60 Percent of the Time, Triple Chance

**What it is** — Burke reports that variant 1 predicts which receiver the quarterback throws to "just about 60%" of the time on the test set; the no-information guess would be one in five, 20 percent, so "we're tripling that information gain" (EeBgUCYhezc [07:48]). Completion percentage is 74 percent when the quarterback throws to the model's recommended receiver and 55 percent when he throws to any other, "a factor of 1.4" (EeBgUCYhezc [08:50]).

He explains why 60 percent is not a poor score: a quarterback "is never going to do this thing twice in a row" given the same situation, so there is natural variance no model removes, and the defense's purpose is to make sure no single receiver is far more favorable than the others, which drives the number down (EeBgUCYhezc [08:19]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why completion differs by 74 versus 55. Inference: the model's top choice is the receiver with the best separation and angles, so agreement partly reflects an easier throw, not that the quarterback's choice is the cause of the difference; the talk does not separate the two.

**When to apply** — When judging any "who gets the ball" or "what happens next" model, state the chance baseline (here 1 in 5) before the accuracy, as the speaker does. Use the 74 versus 55 split to ask whether the model's recommendation carries outcome information.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: the question here is a decision-review one (was this the right target), and a score only earns its place if staff would act on a flagged play.

**When NOT to apply** — The 60 percent is the speaker's own framing of an acceptable result, from one test period (2018 through week 12) and NFL data (EeBgUCYhezc [05:13], [07:48]). There is no confidence interval, and no comparison with a simple baseline other than chance (such as "throw to the open receiver"). Agreement with the model later correlated slightly negatively with production (see [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]]), so high agreement is not a quality score by itself. The talk gives no college or Baylor-level numbers.

**Example** — The speaker's own examples: an easy play where the model gives a crossing receiver an 80 percent target chance (EeBgUCYhezc [09:50]); a checkdown given 8 percent while a deeper open receiver gets 77 percent, which he reads as a probable poor decision (EeBgUCYhezc [10:52]); and a covered receiver the quarterback throws to anyway, where the model agrees because of a velocity advantage and inside leverage, showing that proximity alone does not decide the target (EeBgUCYhezc [11:23], [11:53]).

# "No Research Links Joint Range or Posture to Injury": Said and Disputed in the Q&A

**What it is** — In Q&A an audience member said a full picture of injury risk needs internal load (heart rate load, time in zone), heart rate variability and recovery profiles, hydration, hip mobility asymmetry and pain and soreness, plus RPE, (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:59]). The next sentence, that the number of teams collecting all that data is "pretty much zero," cannot be attributed: the captions carry no speaker labels. The reply, which I read as Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") answering, says "we collect all that data" but disagrees on the hip mobility piece: he said no research has been able to suggest that specific joint ranges of motion or even postures lead to injury or pain, and that you can find correlations in papers that look retrospectively (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:59] to [20:29]). He added that a preseason mobility or posture measure will change as athletes adapt or are given a training intervention, so it would need re-measuring every week, which is possible but hard with about 120 athletes on a collegiate team (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29] to [20:59]). He agreed the full data would be "really helpful."

Where it is contested: the audience member holds that hip mobility asymmetry belongs in the picture; Ward says no research supports a causal link. The disagreement is inside the talk and is not resolved there.

**Why it works** — Ward's stated reason is that retrospective correlations differ from prediction and that measures taken in preseason go stale as athletes adapt (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]). He cites no study for the blanket statement. Inference: "no research has ever" is a strong universal claim made aloud in Q&A and should not be cited as a literature finding.

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask what decision a mobility or posture screen changes before collecting it weekly. Eric's baseline: movement screens are "just collected and referred to for future needs" and change no program decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Eric's baseline: a test that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: this exchange supports Eric's own caution about screens, and by his Q3 rule the screens are candidates to retire or to be given a question.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is contested because the talk itself disagrees. Ward's claim is a universal negative with no citation, and the audience member's view was not rebutted with data. Do not cite it as proof that mobility or posture is irrelevant to injury, or as a reason to stop screening in rehab or return-to-play contexts, which the talk does not address. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]], on asymmetry and injury risk, was not compared in this batch.

**Example** — The speaker's own point: an athlete's hip range measured in preseason and then changed by training means a single preseason value no longer describes him by midseason (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]).

**Related** — [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]] (his wider multifactorial view, which includes intrinsic factors).

# MLB Tommy John surgery counts spiked in 2012 to 2014, then leveled off, but the talk does not link that to the program and also says injuries are rising

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB league office) reports the trend from the public surgery database (caption "baseball heat mass", back to 1974) and from the league's electronic medical record (required of all clubs since 2010; he says league data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [01:39]).

The 2012 to 2014 spike (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [03:12], [03:42], [04:12]):
- Disabled list days for the elbow injury were at an all-time high from 2012 to 2014, a 72% increase over the three years before (the injury is garbled in the caption as "Elvis trees").
- MLB surgeries: the previous high was 22; 36 in 2012; 31 in 2014.
- More of the players were 25 or younger than in any earlier five-year bucket, and many were top young pitchers; recovery is 12 to 16 months.
- The number having a second surgery rose steadily from 1995 to 2014.

The leveling off (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:06], [15:37]): roughly 20 to 25 players a year still have the procedure but "we didn't see the exponential growth" feared; the number of players drafted who had already had the surgery rose steadily to 2014, then was relatively flat over the last three years, though 2016 set an all-time high. In Q&A he says the minor league record shows no linear upward trajectory, "goes up and down" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22], [25:55]).

The speaker does not claim the program caused the leveling off.

Contradiction inside the talk: in the Q&A he compares eras and says "the data kind of suggests ... that injuries are increasing" even though teams are more careful (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:14], the captions are garbled around this sentence); that sits against the leveled-off statements at [14:36] to [15:37]. Another speaker in 2015 (Fleisig) said professional surgeries were still climbing and that youth and high school numbers had been "curved" (caption; read as curbed) a little but were still going up (AgouMNTeyo4 [07:42], [47:52]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for the trend. Inference: a short window after a spike mixes a plateau with ordinary year-to-year noise; one or two years do not make a trend, as the speaker says himself in the Q&A ("tough to judge one or two-year trends", sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22]).

**When to apply** — When a policy is credited for a leveling off in an injury count: check the window length, the denominator and whether the same data also say the opposite.

Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a count of cases without exposure (innings, pitches, athletes at risk) cannot support a causal story about a program.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `contested` because the talk both says the count leveled off and says injuries are increasing, and the 2015 talk describes a still-rising trend; the dates differ, so these may be consistent, but the 2017 Q&A is unclear. The leveling off rests on 2 to 3 years after a spike. There is no exposure denominator or comparison group, and 2016 itself was a record in the draftee count. The speaker works for the league office. Baseball only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: draftees with prior surgery rising to 2014 and then flat, with a 2016 record (sHXuxj3-rbQ [15:06], [15:37]).

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig compares pitchers who came to his center for surgery with pitchers who never had surgery, asking about their backgrounds (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58], [32:30]). He frames the answers as bets: someone who often threw more than 80 pitches in a game: "4 to 1" that he has the scar; someone who pitched more than 8 months a year: "5 to 1" (the "8 months" is caption-dependent); someone who often pitched when fatigued: "36 to 1" (the caption reads "$36 to $1" and "3600%") (AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30], [33:00], [33:31]). He calls the fatigue result "the biggest result I found" in all his studies and says "you could throw everything else away" and keep it: pitchers who keep pitching after they are fatigued end up with serious injury (AgouMNTeyo4 [33:31]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig gives no mechanism. Inference: fatigue is a state in which each additional pitch is thrown with less control, which would plausibly add stress; the speaker does not say this, and he measured history, not mechanics, in this comparison.

**When to apply** — When the question is which exposure is the most modifiable for a throwing athlete's history: fatigue behavior (continuing when tired) and volume (pitches per game, months per year). Pair with the prospective 100-innings result rather than using the odds alone.

Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed); the eye flags where to look and data then investigates ("There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further," interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, and are kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: the speaker's "fatigued" is a history item the athlete reports; Eric's survey experience is a reason to doubt a self-reported fatigue score used daily.

**When NOT to apply** — These are retrospective odds from recalled history, not a prospective rate: there is no control for who tells the story, for when pitchers were asked, or for who came in for surgery in the first place. The speaker states the odds as spoken wagers and gives no sample size, no confidence interval and no definition of "often" or "fatigued". He says in his Q&A that fatigue cannot be measured scientifically in the moment. The caption wording of the three odds ("8 months", "$36 to $1") is uncertain. Do not treat 36 to 1 as an individual risk score or transfer it to football. The speaker advises MLB, Little League, USA Baseball and a device company.

**Example** — The speaker's own device: he imagines half a room with elbow scars and half without, asks each person whether he often pitched when fatigued, and says a "yes" is a 36 to 1 bet that the person is in the scar group (paraphrase of AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30] to [33:31]; the caption is garbled).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]]; [[heuristic--fatigue-is-individual-read-it-next-day-with-trainer-knowledge]] (his Q&A answer on how to see fatigue); [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] (Old Bull).

# One Model Ranks Quarterback Highest and Center Second in Positional Variance

**What it is** — In Paul Sabin's 2019 college data the quarterback's position variance is "by far the furthest out," and the center is second, a result he calls somewhat surprising because no one on TV says it, though his own experience said the center is the next most important position (oZsFyPGij0U [12:56], [13:26]). He says he showed it to several Division I coaches and staffs (oZsFyPGij0U [13:26], [13:56]). His explanation is a hypothesis: the center calls the blocking scheme, so a wrong assignment by a tackle may be the center's error and would not show on film, while the data show a good center's replacement hurts team outcomes more than a tackle's replacement does (oZsFyPGij0U [13:56], [14:27]). Other points he makes:
- Most of the other positions are "really close together" and could depend on team and scheme (oZsFyPGij0U [14:27]).
- Tight end here means hand on the ground; a standing player in the slot counts as a slot receiver (oZsFyPGij0U [14:27], [14:57]).
- The ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with defensive line and tight end "not that important," quarterbacks always first, and much uncertainty around running backs (oZsFyPGij0U [14:57], [15:28]).
- A questioner asked whether the center effect is continuity; he says it is part of it but the effect differs for centers versus other positions, and the cause is "a question to be studied" (oZsFyPGij0U [23:09], [23:39]).
- Centers' ratings also track team success, less strongly; Clemson's center was top-rated going into 2019 while Trevor Lawrence was not the top-rated quarterback (oZsFyPGij0U [24:42], [25:13]).
- He does not know why slot cornerbacks rate high (oZsFyPGij0U [25:13]).

These are posterior distributions on the variance, so a more uncertain position can have a wide distribution without being "less important" (oZsFyPGij0U [26:45], [27:15]). For the NFL he used a 90 percent interval line instead of the density plot (oZsFyPGij0U [27:15]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism for the center is the scheme-calling hypothesis above; he does not test it. For the other positions he gives none. Inference: a high-variance position is one where the spread between the best and replacement player in the model is large, which is a statement about outcomes in his data, not about job difficulty.

**When to apply** — As a reasonableness check on how a staff weights positions, not as a recruiting rule. Inference: compare the ordering against the spread of PFF grades by position group at Baylor, as the applications note suggests. Eric's baseline: no direct link; the method baseline is silent on position valuation.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: no out-of-sample validation is shown, and the center result rests on an untested explanation. The ordering is an artifact of one model with its priors and its position definitions (see [[framework--position-variance-and-informative-priors-in-football-plus-minus]]); the model gives each position its own variance by design, though the speaker says the position parameters are estimated across all positions (oZsFyPGij0U [11:24]). He does not say how strongly the prior pushes the estimate, so how much of the ordering is data and how much is structure is not shown. The tight end definition is nonstandard. Data are 2019 college and 2007 onward NFL; do not apply NFL stability to Baylor depth-chart decisions. Do not read the result as causal.

**Example** — The speaker's own: going into 2019 the model's highest-rated college center was Clemson's (oZsFyPGij0U [24:42]).

**Related** — [[framework--position-variance-and-informative-priors-in-football-plus-minus]]; [[heuristic--plausibility-checks-for-a-player-value-model-without-ground-truth]].

# Single-Club Load Models Predicted Injury Poorly on Unseen Data

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") cites a tweet by Luke Bourne (caption spelling "Luke borne"), a co-author of his paper, saying the sports science industry states "we predict injuries" while the research community says injury prediction is hard and unresolved (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39]). The tweet linked a paper from "David Carey's group out of Australia" (caption spelling). Ward's account of it: the group built predictive models of training load and injury in Australian football, tested them on unseen data, and concluded that models built from a single club's load data showed poor ability to predict injuries on previously unseen data, so they are limited as daily decision tools for practitioners (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]). No accuracy figures are given in the talk.

Ward adds a contrast: technology companies tell practitioners to "dump your data in" and injury will be predicted, while the people collecting the data know how hard it is to get it clean and coded properly, and injury is multifactorial (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond injury being multifactorial and data quality being hard (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]). Inference: a model fit on one club's data may be capturing that club's practices and noise, which would fail on new data, but the talk does not say this.

**When to apply** — As the standard to ask of any vendor or paper claiming prediction: was it tested on unseen data, and at more than one club? Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is followed, and ACWR is looked at but not trusted (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this is outside support for that decision to avoid formal models.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Ward's secondhand description of one Australian football study, not a first-hand reading of it. The sport (Australian football) and the data source (single club) bound it; the talk does not say it holds for multi-club data or for American football. It is a statement about daily decision tools, not about whether load relates to injury at all; Ward's own study reports associations (see the case-study entry).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the sports science industry says "we predict injuries," the research community says it is hard, and the cited Australian group's out-of-sample test supports the research community (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]] (check 6). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]] in the research-paper library; its title matches the paper Ward describes, but this batch did not open it, so verify they are the same study.

# Players, parents and coaches overestimate what Tommy John surgery does

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB, director of league economics and strategy, sHXuxj3-rbQ [00:02], [00:37]) says a perception had grown that the surgery is always successful and returns a pitcher within a year throwing harder, and that players should have it before an injury to improve performance (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [05:46]). A survey designed by a Yankees physician (caption "dr. mod"; the 2015 talk's caption "Dr Ahmad ... the New York Yankees doctor", probably the same survey, unconfirmed) went to youth players, coaches and parents asking how successful the surgery is, how long it takes, and whether the player will throw harder (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46]). Results as the speaker reports:
- More than half of high school players thought a player should have the surgery without an actual elbow injury.
- More than half of college players thought pitch speed increases afterward (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]).

Fleisig's 2015 account of what appears to be the same survey gives different numbers: about two-thirds of respondents guessed about 60 percent make it back, about a third thought velocity goes up, a third to a half thought performance improves, and 25 to 50 percent thought surgery makes sense in some cases even without an injury, which he calls "frightening" (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:30], [19:01], [19:33]). He adds that pro teams sometimes tell him a hurt pitcher should "just go get a surgery and get it over with", which is "not the right attitude", and that doctors say surgery is a last resort (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:00]). The two talks give different splits by group; do not harmonize them.

The speaker's response: the third part of the Pitch Smart program (see the program entry) gives accurate information so that players see surgery as "something I want to avoid, not something I want to have" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:55]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for why the perception formed; DeAngelo lists it as one of the league's 2014 concerns (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:10]). Inference: when a rare success story (a star pitcher returning at full velocity) is visible and the outcome distribution is not, a perception gap forms, and measuring it is the first step in correcting it.

**When to apply** — As a method: before a recovery or rehab education effort, survey the athletes, coaches and parents on what they believe about outcomes, and compare to published outcomes. Also as a caution when staff or athletes describe a procedure as performance-enhancing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's four operating principles include Research and Development and Performance Team Collaboration (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and in return to performance it contributes "Testing and progression", with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4). The baseline holds no education survey of athletes' beliefs.

**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitchers' beliefs about one surgery; the survey sample sizes, response rates and wording are not shown in either talk. The speaker says "all of our research and all the research of the medical community" shows the beliefs are incorrect, but Fleisig reports that one of three studies found performance improved after surgery (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39]), so "incorrect" on performance is contested (see the return-rate entry). The speaker is a league-office official describing the league's program. Do not use belief percentages from one talk as a Baylor estimate.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the survey result that more than half of high school players thought surgery without injury was reasonable (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46], [06:17]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 talk: what the outcome studies show); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]].

# Charted Grades as Labels, Tracking Data as Predictors

**What it is** — Eric Eager (introduced as being from Pro Football Focus, PFF) argues that football analytics has three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, player tracking) that are mostly used one at a time, and that they enhance one another when combined (Q3i3FOC-dPE [01:33], [04:12]). His design, used in three cases: the hand-charted measure is the training target and tracking data supplies the predictors.
- **Pass rush:** charted pressure (and, in a second model, charted win rate) is the label; predictors are play-level context, the defender's position at the snap, charted position labels, and how fast he leaves the ball in the first second, in the vertical direction and as straight-line distance (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:16], [06:47], [07:18]).
- **Linebacker coverage:** the coverage grade is unstable, so he derives a tracking-based trait, play-action "bite distance" (see [[claim--bite-distance-under-expected-is-steadier-than-coverage-grade]]).
- **Receiver deep speed:** speed over the play predicts the PFF grade on go and corner routes (see [[case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown]]).

PFF charters grade every NFL and college game by hand; the NFL's tracking data comes from chips in the shoulder pads and ball (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:08], [02:40]). The model for pressure is XGBoost, "an ensemble" of decision trees, and returns a per-play pressure probability, not only a yes or no (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:47], [07:48]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning: the charted outcome carries what the hand grader judged and the tracking data adds a continuous, repeatable measure of athletic behavior (Q3i3FOC-dPE [09:19], [10:20]). He gives no further mechanism. Inference: the charted label supplies what counts as success on a play, and tracking supplies how the player moved, so each repairs the other's gap.

**When to apply** — When one data source labels outcomes but is subjective or coarse, and another measures movement. Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (Explicit, SportSmith article). Inference: this design reuses data already collected, which fits that cost rule. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — The slides are not visible and most R-squared values, sample sizes, seasons and play counts are not in the captions (Q3i3FOC-dPE transcript). The speaker works for PFF and presents PFF tools as results, a commercial view. The tracking data is league-wide shoulder-pad data, which a single college program does not hold (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:40]). PFF grades come in half-point steps from negative two (caption wording) and graders are not asked to do context math (Q3i3FOC-dPE [26:36], [27:07]). Supported only where the speaker reports a method with a result; see [[claim--expected-pressure-rate-adds-to-pressure-rate-in-predicting-sacks]].

**Example** — The speaker's pass-rush case: the vertical distance covered in the first second is the most important variable for a pressure (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:47]).

# DeepQB: Receiver-Level Inputs and Four Model Variants

**What it is** — Brian Burke (name as stated in the host introduction, EeBgUCYhezc [00:00]) presents DeepQB, a feed-forward neural network, which he calls "a relatively vanilla type of deep learning application", applied to NFL Next Gen Stats (NGS) player tracking data (EeBgUCYhezc [03:42], [04:12]). One architecture answers four questions (EeBgUCYhezc [04:12], [04:43]):

1. Variant 1: which of the five eligible receivers the quarterback targets (target probability).
2. Variant 2: expected yards on the play.
3. Variant 3: outcome probability (complete, incomplete, intercepted).
4. Variant 4: variant 1 tailored to one quarterback (see [[case-study--deepqb-quarterback-specific-transfer-learning-did-not-work]]).

**Inputs.** The feature vector is arranged by the five eligible receivers: absolute position, position relative to the quarterback, velocity, orientation, and receiver type (wide receiver, tight end, running back) (EeBgUCYhezc [06:15]). It adds the nearest two defenders in coverage (absolute and relative position, velocities, accelerations, orientations), then play context: game state, down, distance, yard line, play action, a 1/0 flag for quarterback duress, and quarterback velocity at release (EeBgUCYhezc [06:15], [06:46]). He stresses that the NGS data are "extremely clean" and available about 10 seconds after the play (EeBgUCYhezc [05:44]).

**Data and split.** More than 45,000 targeted passes only (the model only sees whom the quarterback chose to throw to), drawn from 2016 through 2018 through week 12 of 2018, split into training, validation and test sets; all reported results are from the test set, 2018 through week 12 (EeBgUCYhezc [04:43], [05:13]).

**Mirror-image augmentation.** Each play is also included flipped left-right in the training set, to teach symmetry. The speaker names the flaw himself: quarterback handedness (EeBgUCYhezc [06:46], [07:16]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the single architecture: he found "the architecture of the model was optimum for a wide variety of applications" because it suited the structure of the data, so the same network could be asked different questions (EeBgUCYhezc [04:12]). He gives no mechanism for why mirroring helps beyond the symmetry intent. Inference: arranging inputs per receiver lets the same weights score each of the five targets, which is why one model can serve several outputs.

**When to apply** — As a reference design when someone proposes a model of a passer's decision from play-level positional data: check that the inputs describe each option (receiver and nearest defenders), the context (down, distance, duress), and that results are scored only on a held-out period.

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: this model needs league-grade per-play tracking at scale (45,000+ passes), which is a large collection cost; Eric's baseline contains no football position-tracking method, so there is nothing of his own to compare it with.

**When NOT to apply** — NFL tracking data of a quality Baylor does not hold; the speaker built this on 2016 to 2018 NFL passes. It sees positions, speed and orientation only: "no vertical information" and no "hands" (EeBgUCYhezc [22:01]). He calls the project "a big proof of concept" built on early choices "to make sure that this would work" (EeBgUCYhezc [23:32]). Inference: a college program with a few hundred hand-tagged plays is not the same problem; his own individualized variant failed for too little data per passer (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a play where the model gives the receiver the quarterback chose a 15 percent target probability while another receiver "coming open" has a higher one (EeBgUCYhezc [10:21]).

# Setting an impact-alert threshold: the S-curve and the sideline test it depends on

**What it is** — The speaker's way of reasoning about a helmet, headband or mouthpiece sensor with a red-light and green-light alert (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Risk of concussion against linear acceleration is an S-curve: he knows of no concussion at 10 G, and concussion "everyone's going to get" at 300 G, with only a curve in between, so any alert line is arbitrary (npgdKKdJSww [08:04], [08:35]). He walks the trade-off:
- Line at 50 G: the light "going off all the time", and every flagged athlete needs an evaluation.
- Line at 100 G: fewer alerts, but concussions at 60 or 70 G are missed.
- Line at 150 G: "once every few games", and "you're really not helping anybody" because most concussions happen at lower levels (npgdKKdJSww [08:35], [09:06]).

The alert is only usable if the follow-up test is fast. He wants a sideline test under one minute so the line can be set low (he mentions 80 or 100 G) without disrupting the game (npgdKKdJSww [09:06], [09:36]). The existing 20-minute evaluation (caption "SC stat too", likely SCAT2) "has never been validated" and its parts cannot decide return to play alone, and at a low yield (he says "10%" actually concussed) "no one's going to use it" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36], [10:06]). The one fast test he calls promising is King-Devick: two published papers (boxers, MMA fighters, college athletes at Penn) found concussions in under one minute by comparing to baseline (npgdKKdJSww [11:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the logic of false alarms against misses but no data on any particular line. Inference: the threshold choice sets a false-alarm rate, and the false-alarm rate is only tolerable if the confirmation step is cheap, which makes the confirmation step the binding design constraint.

**When to apply** — Before anyone proposes alerts from impact sensors, GPS-unit collision counts or any single-number flag: state the line, the expected alerts per game, who evaluates each one, and how long that takes.

Eric's baseline: a measurement earns its place only if it answers a question someone has ("If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place," interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit), and data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: an alert with no cheap follow-up fails both tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker discloses a financial relationship with the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]), and the "promising" claim rests on two papers he does not name. The 10 G and 300 G anchors are stated without a source. The 2012 sensors measured linear acceleration only, and the SCAT2 and King-Devick remarks may be out of date; check current guidelines. The caption "45C evaluation" at [11:41] to [12:12] is garbled. Return-to-play decisions belong to Athletic Medicine.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a line of 80 to 100 G with a one-minute baseline-comparison test, so that "you know immediately whether or not they can go back in" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36]). He says this does not exist yet.

# Null-Model Simulation: Check Whether a Risk Metric Can Look Predictive When It Has No Effect

**What it is** — A way to test a monitoring metric before trusting it. The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) built it for the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR). The steps as they describe them: (1) take real session-load data from a team, in their case one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (the captions say "Syria" and "Serria", probably Serie A, unconfirmed) (TIRINmtZOu0 [12:11]); (2) assume a "null model" in which everything leading into a session is irrelevant and only the intensity of the current session changes injury probability (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:12], [13:43]); (3) simulate whole seasons of injuries under that rule, 1,000 seasons per sport (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43]); (4) run the same test the published studies run (a chi-square test of ACWR against injury) on the simulated seasons (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:13], [14:43]); (5) if the metric still "predicts" injury, the usual analysis cannot tell the metric's effect from the schedule's effect.

**Why it works** — The simulation fixes the true cause by construction, so any association between ACWR and injury that appears must come from how the data are structured, not from ACWR. The speakers' account of that structure is in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The speakers do not describe the simulation code or how session loads were drawn; that detail is in their paper and was not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**When to apply** — Before adopting any ratio, rolling-window or flag as an injury-risk score, or when someone reports a clean association between a monitoring metric and injury. Inference: the same design can be run on a department's own load data, with the null set to "only the planned intensity of today's session matters," to see how much apparent signal the schedule alone manufactures. Eric's baseline: "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything" and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit). Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has" has no place (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); this check is a cheap way to ask whether a flag answers one.

**When NOT to apply** — The talk reports the result for two teams in two sports, with no stated roster size, injury count or load metric, so the size of the artifact in a college football season is unknown. A simulation shows that an artifact is possible and of a certain size under the assumed null; it does not show the published studies are wrong, and the speakers say so (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49]). It cannot be run without session-level load for every player, and the null (only today's intensity matters) is the speakers' assumption, not a measured fact. Single conference presentation; the adjusted analysis was not shown.

**Example** — The speakers' own: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport in which ACWR was irrelevant by design still produced an extremely significant chi-square result, and an apparent injury-risk increase of 6.8% (Italian team) and 10.5% (NFL team), figures read from auto captions (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43], [15:15]). # Position-Specific Variance and Informative Priors in a Football Plus-Minus Model

**What it is** — Paul Sabin's fix for the co-presence problem has four parts, all stated as a Bayesian ridge-style model fit in Stan.
1. **Position variance multiplier.** A parameter he calls S_J (caption notation) multiplies the prior variance by position. "If a position has high variance it is more important": the best player at a high-variance position is worth much more than the best at a position where the best and replacement levels are close (oZsFyPGij0U [09:19], [09:49]). The key premise is that even the best offensive lineman is worth less than the best quarterback (oZsFyPGij0U [08:49]).
2. **Informative shrinkage target.** Ordinary ridge assumes a player with few snaps is near average; he says that is probably wrong because players who do not play much are usually not good (oZsFyPGij0U [09:49]). He shrinks toward draft rank for NFL rookies, recruiting data for college players, and "what we thought you were last year" for veterans (oZsFyPGij0U [10:21]).
3. **Multi-position players** get a snap-weighted average across positions (he uses Taysom Hill as the case, "like 10 different positions"), with position set by alignment (oZsFyPGij0U [10:52], [11:24], [26:15]).
4. **Heavy tails.** A Student-t prior (eight degrees of freedom, "no magic in that number," chosen as a speed trade-off because the models are run after games) lets the best players sit further from average than a normal prior would (oZsFyPGij0U [11:24], [11:54], [12:25]).

The only inputs are position, who is on the field, and down, distance and yard line for expected points (oZsFyPGij0U [20:05]). NFL runs finish after each game window, so values are ready the next morning; college is slower because a data provider tracks manually (oZsFyPGij0U [12:25]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the intuition (position importance differs, so equal priors waste information) but no formal argument. Inference: position-specific variance lets the model attribute more of a shared outcome to a quarterback than to a lineman when the two cannot be separated by their snaps alone.

**When to apply** — As a template for building a single value number when players are always co-present: add a prior that encodes known structure (position, pedigree) rather than assuming everyone is average. Inference: the low-snap shrinkage idea is relevant to any Baylor grade built on small snap counts, where pulling toward recruiting or prior-year information is more defensible than pulling toward the mean. Eric's baseline: no direct link found in the method baseline, which has nothing on recruiting grading or PFF data.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested. The speaker shows no out-of-sample test; the evidence is plausibility checks (see [[heuristic--plausibility-checks-for-a-player-value-model-without-ground-truth]]). The prior itself can mislead: last year's prior held back Joe Burrow in the college model (oZsFyPGij0U [17:30]), and the speaker plans a predictive and an in-season version for that reason ([[heuristic--separate-predictive-and-descriptive-versions-of-a-player-value-model]]). The model ignores assignments, scheme and coaching (oZsFyPGij0U [20:05]), and values depend on position labels set by alignment. Do not reuse his eight degrees of freedom or his priors as validated settings; he gives no tuning evidence. College results depend on manual tracking data that Baylor may not have.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a college quarterback and his linemen on the field about 98 to 99 percent of plays are still separated, and the plots show the quarterback and average-line values correlated but not tightly (oZsFyPGij0U [18:03], [18:34]).

# A Draft Lottery That Depends on When Results Happen, With Odds Frozen at a Data-Chosen Point

**What it is** — Evan Monroe says that if the lottery depends on when wins and losses occur, not only on final rankings, it can favor the worst team and remove tanking incentives (-6pe_zOKCig [09:15]). The policy (-6pe_zOKCig [11:55] to [13:26]):
1. After every game, re-estimate each team's probability of finishing last, conditional on results so far; at the start of the season, with equal ability assumed, every team has an equal chance.
2. Set draft odds to match those probabilities, so a long early losing streak raises a team's odds.
3. Freeze the odds at a stopping time chosen dynamically from what happens that season, not a fixed date, since the incentives to win and lose depend on when the streak happens and on who is in the draft.
Early games count more because "uncertainty is actually a good thing" if you are giving a prize to a team that does badly: at the start nobody knows where they will finish, so early losses are a good signal of a bad team and incentives to lose are weak then (-6pe_zOKCig [16:30], [21:03]). The point is to freeze when, in the model, the incentive to win would start to be dominated by the incentive to lose (-6pe_zOKCig [17:00], [17:30]). He says the process removes incentives to tank within a season in the model (-6pe_zOKCig [13:26]). The results he shows come from back-tests: see [[case-study--1989-miami-heat-back-test-of-the-time-dependent-lottery]] and [[claim--rule-degrades-when-the-prize-is-worth-as-much-as-the-playoffs]].

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism: the lottery tracks the posterior chance of finishing last, so the best-supported worst team gets the highest odds, while the freeze point sits where late losing would no longer pay (-6pe_zOKCig [13:26], [17:30]). Proofs are in the paper and not shown.

**When to apply** — As a pattern for any ranking or reward that distorts behavior late: weight early, low-stakes evidence more and stop updating when the incentive to game would dominate. Eric's baseline: no direct link found for rankings; see [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]] for the audit question. Inference: early baseline captures taken before athletes know what a number will change are cleaner reference points, as the applications note suggests.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: back-tests in the speaker's own model, with no real-world trial (the speaker works from a paper in a competition). It depends on a league forecast that accounts for known factors (an injured star returning, trades); if a team knows something the league's forecast does not, gaming remains possible (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33], [23:03]). It may increase the incentive to rebuild over several seasons, which the model does not cover (-6pe_zOKCig [13:58], [23:33]). Only the first pick is modeled; the extension to a full draft is in an appendix (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39], [27:10]). The freeze point is stated inconsistently in the captions (see the case study).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 1989 Miami Heat losing streak at the start of the season (-6pe_zOKCig [16:00], [16:30]).

**Related** — [[claim--lottery-on-final-ranking-alone-cannot-favor-worst-team-without-tank-incentive]]; [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]]; [[claim--model-limits-forecast-gaps-rebuilding-and-single-pick-scope]].
