# When the Output Is a Probability, Pick the Better-Calibrated Model

**What it is** — For the pressure score, Hong chose a random forest over "a complex neural network based or Transformer based model", because "model calibration" matters for a continuous score and the forest had better expected calibration error and maximum calibration error (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26], [11:58], [12:28]). No calibration values are given.

He also notes an evaluation difficulty: a continuous pressure score is "kind of hard to evaluate", so he used a proxy, the maximum pressure a rusher or team puts on a passer, compared against PFF hurry, hit and sack labels, and reports "great accuracy" and better accuracy against hits and sacks, with a disparity across player groups and room to improve (the captions are garbled here; 1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26], [11:58]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states calibration as the reason and gives no mechanism for why forests calibrate better than deep models here. Inference: a score read as a probability by a coach (for example, "70 percent chance this rusher gets home") is only honest if stated probabilities match observed frequencies.

**When to apply** — When model output will be shown as a probability or compared with a threshold (the talk uses a 75 percent "pressure zone" at 1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]): compare candidate models on calibration error as well as accuracy, and prefer the simpler one when it calibrates better.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: a simple, inspectable model that Applied Performance staff can explain to coaches fits that rule better than a model nobody can interrogate.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no error values, no comparison table shown, only the speaker's statement. It applies to a probability output, and does not mean forests beat neural networks in general. The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc) used a feed-forward network and reported a calibration chart "fairly well calibrated" ([[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]), so calibration is achievable with a neural network; the two talks do not compare.

**Example** — The speaker's choice itself: random forest over neural or Transformer models for the pressure score (1nt8hK2oYrE [12:28]).

# Keep a Predictive Version and a Descriptive Version of a Player Value Model

**What it is** — Paul Sabin found that his prior, built from the previous year's performance, kept Joe Burrow from ranking first in the 2019 college season despite a "fantastic year": he was good but not great the year before (caption "Joe burrowed") (oZsFyPGij0U [17:30]). His planned change is two versions. A predictive version uses previous results as the prior and answers what a trade or free-agent signing is worth going into 2020. A descriptive version uses only that season's numbers (box-score priors, as in ESPN's real plus-minus) and answers who had the best 2019 season, because "those are two different stories" (oZsFyPGij0U [17:30], [20:35], [21:06]). He also plans expected turnover points instead of plain expected points (oZsFyPGij0U [20:05], [20:35]).

**When to apply** — Whenever one number is asked to serve both an award question and a roster-decision question. Inference: a Baylor portal or recruiting grade is a predictive question and should lean on prior-year information; an end-of-season recognition is descriptive and should not be held down by the prior. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one example (Burrow) and an intention, not a tested design. Burrow is a single player and the caption spelling is garbled, though the sense is clear. If the metric measures something systematic about talent or production, it will correlate and travel with the player from year to year and from team to team (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:29]). Their result: open score is the most stable of the three receiver components, "about as consistent as batting averages" in baseball (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:59]). # Training Load Gives Risk Context, Not Injury Prediction

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") frames his result as associated risk that practitioners can use "to build appropriate training sessions that are logical and hopefully mitigate injury," not as prediction before a session (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]). He says practitioners can combine volume and intensity findings with the heuristics they have built over years of designing sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23]). To make a model truly predictive he says it would need much more than load: "we're probably really naive" to think only load factors raise non-contact injury risk; there are intrinsic factors the athlete brings, extrinsic factors of the session, their interactions, and how those interactions change as players adapt or maladapt across a season (TbYgc6_qQzo [17:24] to [17:54]).

Q&A adds two cautions. An audience member argued that training is "endogenous to effort," so correlations could reflect players who try hard in both practice and games, and that random assignment would address it; Ward agreed it would help if a coach would allow it, and noted the group also tracks perceived effort but did not use it in this paper (TbYgc6_qQzo [18:24] to [19:27]). Underreporting of pain by athletes is, he says, one of the most complex limits in collegiate and professional sport (TbYgc6_qQzo [24:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is multifactorial causation, as above. He gives no data that other factors would improve prediction; that is his position, not a result. Inference: treating load as one risk input fits that position and avoids implying a certainty the model lacks.

**When to apply** — When a load report is used in a conversation with coaches about a practice plan. Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q6). Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through load progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: both fit Ward's stance that a load measure informs the coach's judgment rather than replacing it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's stance, supported by the limits of his own study (29 injuries, one team, one season) but not tested as a decision approach. It gives no rule for how much weight to give load against other information. The endogeneity concern was raised by an audience member and only partly answered. Eric's baseline: no formal risk model is followed (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: that makes this principle a description of current practice, not a new method for Baylor.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a session scoring high on impacts is a risk factor to weigh against what a coach knows, not a signal to cancel work (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51], [16:23]).

# The Training Schedule Can Create an ACWR to Injury Association Without ACWR Causing Injury

**What it is** — The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) propose a causal structure, drawn as a directed acyclic graph (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10]). The published analyses compute ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [10:10], [10:40]). The speakers add a missing third variable: the schedule drives both ACWR and the intensity of the upcoming session, and session intensity drives injury (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10], [11:41]). If the last seven days were hard, ACWR is high, and the next session is also likely to be hard (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:41]). Their density plots show that when athletes are in the "danger zone" of ACWR, upcoming session loads are higher than when they are in the "sweet spot" (TIRINmtZOu0 [16:16], [16:47]). Schedule features named: training camp, where load jumps from zero to a lot, international breaks, and the weekly cycle (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39], [16:47], [17:18]). They open with an ice cream and drowning example of confounding (TIRINmtZOu0 [03:33]).

**Why it works** — The structure is a standard confounder: a shared cause makes two variables move together. The speakers show two things: the simulation in [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]], and that in their real data the ACWR association goes from "highly significant to non-significant" once same-session load is accounted for, in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). The adjusted effect sizes and models are "in the paper" and were not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). The speakers give no physiological mechanism for why session intensity raises injury risk; they treat it as given. Inference: a high-intensity session in itself being the injury exposure is consistent with how they frame it, but the talk does not test it.

**When to apply** — Whenever a load metric computed from the days before a session is correlated with an outcome in that session. Inference: check whether the metric also predicts the load of the session itself; if it does, the metric may be a proxy for that load. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and progressions are kept smooth. The talk does not contradict this: it says the ratio may reflect the schedule and leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested. This is the speakers' explanation, supported by one simulation and unshown real-data adjustments from two teams. The speakers themselves say they have not disproved the earlier papers and that the explanation is "another really good explanation" (TIRINmtZOu0 [19:19]). Existing library: Griffin 2020, a systematic review of 22 studies, reports ACWR associations with non-contact injury and recommends use inside a broader multifactorial monitoring system, so it does not read the association as pure artifact; Impellizzeri 2020 agrees with the artifact reading on Serie A data. Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:42]). Do not use this entry to claim that training load is irrelevant to injury.

**Example** — The speakers' own: training camp, where coaches "purposefully increase training demands" and where the literature also finds the highest injury risk, raises ACWR and session intensity together (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39]).
